place.unraid_intro: Everything Unraid knows about itself lives in /boot/config.
place.docker_intro: Containers from Unraid's Docker page are described by an XML template on the flash — a text file with image, folders, ports and variables. Add the container again from it (Apps → Previous Apps) and it is back with all its settings. Its data lives in appdata.
place.compose_intro: A compose stack is described in a text file (compose.yaml — .yml is the same, just spelled shorter): which containers belong to it, with which image, folders and ports. The override file adds to or changes that without touching the original; the .env holds values such as passwords or paths that the compose file fills in — which is why it deserves extra care. The Compose Manager keeps a folder per stack on the flash; "indirect" stacks point to a folder elsewhere.
place.vms_intro: Everything that makes a VM — its XML, the UEFI variables (NVRAM) and the TPM state — lives inside libvirt.img, which is mounted at /etc/libvirt while the VM service runs. The virtual disks live in the domains share.
place.vms_more: Details per VM — what you need to move each one →
place.scripts_intro: Every user script is a folder on the flash with its script; the schedules of all of them are in one file.
place.office_intro: The office itself, its runtime data (state, who works here) and the backup engine's settings, logs and database dumps.

boot.pool: This server doesn't boot from a USB stick but from the ZFS pool «{pool}» — a {layout} over {devices}, started from the EFI partitions {efi}. Everything Unraid knows about itself is there in /boot/config.

boot.other: Everything Unraid knows about itself lives in /boot/config ({fs}).
boot.restore: Getting it back: install Unraid fresh on a boot medium (Unraid USB Creator or Unraid's own installer), then copy the config folder back — the array, shares, Docker templates, plugins and the license key file come back with it.
boot.degraded: The boot pool {pool} isn't healthy ({state}) — check it on the Main page.
boot.single: The boot pool has only one disk — if it fails, Unraid doesn't start until it's restored.
boot.license_tpm: The license ({file}) is bound to the TPM of this mainboard: on the same mainboard there is nothing to transfer. Only a new mainboard needs a license transfer (Tools → Registration).
boot.license_flash: The license ({file}) is bound to the boot stick's GUID ({guid}): with a new stick, transfer it to the new GUID (Tools → Registration).
boot.license_other: The license ({file}) belongs to a GUID that is neither this stick's nor this TPM's — check it under Tools → Registration.
help.title: How to read this page
help.tiles_text: Each tile is a place with files that matter. Its label shows the weakest protection among them (the system log in RAM and Docker's image data don't count — they are rebuilt anyway). A click opens the paths with their size and protection.
help.copy_text: Puts the path on the clipboard — for a terminal, the Files Viewer or a note for the day you need it.
help.rows_text: A click anywhere on a row unfolds its details; «Unfold all» opens every row of the tab. ⋯ has more for some rows.
help.search_text: Searches every tab at once — names, paths, images, IPs. The numbers on the tabs show the hits.
help.tour_text: Reads everything again right now; otherwise she looks again when the page is opened and her last look is older than 10 minutes.
help.asleep_text: Ms. Whereabouts never wakes a sleeping disk on her own. What only an array disk could tell her stays unknown until it is awake; sizes of array shares are measured only when you ask. «Wake sleeping disks» next to Tour wakes them all at once for one tour.
help.labels_text: How Mr. Backupsy protects a path, after the rules of his settings:
wake_title: For this tour only: wakes every sleeping disk at once and reads everything — where shares really are, whether paths on the array exist, VM disks there. Unraid spins them down again after its delay.

adv.title: If I were you …
adv.sub: What I would do differently — advice, not errors. «I know, thanks» hides a tip in this browser; it comes back when something changes.

adv.system_array.title: On the array: {names}
adv.system_array.why: Docker's and the VMs' own things belong on a pool (SSD/NVMe): on the array every container and VM gets slow, and the disks never get to sleep. In the share's settings set the primary storage to a pool and the secondary to none, then let the mover bring the files over (with Docker and VMs stopped).

adv.mover.title.one: The mover has no schedule — {names} relies on it
adv.mover.title.other: The mover has no schedule — {n} shares rely on it: {names}

adv.mover.why: These shares write to a pool first and the mover is meant to take things to the array (or back). Without a schedule it only runs when started by hand — the pool fills up. Settings → Scheduler → Mover Settings. (If something else starts the mover for you, «I know, thanks».)

adv.exclusive_off.title.one: Exclusive shares are off — {names} would qualify
adv.exclusive_off.title.other: Exclusive shares are off — {n} shares would qualify: {names}

adv.exclusive_off.why.one: Psst — this share lives on a single pool and nowhere else, and still every byte squeezes through Unraid's FUSE layer (shfs) under /mnt/user. As an exclusive share /mnt/user/… becomes a link straight to the pool, so reads and writes skip that layer — noticeably faster, most of all with many small files. Docker and VM paths like /mnt/user/appdata keep working: they go through the link. The setting can only be changed with the array stopped (Docker and VMs stop with it): Main → Array Operation → Stop, then Settings → Global Share Settings → «Permit exclusive shares»: Yes → Apply, and start the array again. Unraid decides when the array starts — a share with a folder on another disk or pool too stays as it is. (For exclusive shares Unraid ignores «Minimum free space».)
adv.exclusive_off.why.other: Psst — these shares live on a single pool and nowhere else, and still every byte squeezes through Unraid's FUSE layer (shfs) under /mnt/user. As exclusive shares /mnt/user/… becomes a link straight to the pool, so reads and writes skip that layer — noticeably faster, most of all with many small files. Docker and VM paths like /mnt/user/appdata keep working: they go through the link. The setting can only be changed with the array stopped (Docker and VMs stop with it): Main → Array Operation → Stop, then Settings → Global Share Settings → «Permit exclusive shares»: Yes → Apply, and start the array again. Unraid decides when the array starts — a share with a folder on another disk or pool too stays as it is. (For exclusive shares Unraid ignores «Minimum free space».)

adv.exclusive_elsewhere.why: Well, well — a folder of the same name on another pool or disk (in brackets). That alone, even an empty one, keeps Unraid from linking the share straight to its pool: it stays in the slower FUSE layer. What lies in that folder is part of the share: move it onto the share's pool (Unraid's file manager: Browse), or delete the folder if it is empty. Then stop and start the array once (Main → Array Operation) — Unraid decides when it starts. Fix Common Problems reports such folders too — let it check again after tidying up (Settings → User Utilities → Fix Common Problems → Rescan).

adv.exclusive_unclear.title.one: {names} isn't exclusive — and I can't see why
adv.exclusive_unclear.title.other: {n} shares aren't exclusive — and I can't see why: {names}

adv.exclusive_unclear.why.one: Now that's a mystery: by its settings it qualifies, I see its folder only on its own pool, and still Unraid says «Exclusive access: No». {maybe} Unraid decides when the array starts: once that is sorted out, stop and start the array (Main → Array Operation).
adv.exclusive_unclear.why.other: Now that's a mystery: by their settings they qualify, I see their folder only on their own pool, and still Unraid says «Exclusive access: No». {maybe} Unraid decides when the array starts: once that is sorted out, stop and start the array (Main → Array Operation).

adv.exclusive_unclear.asleep: Perhaps a folder of the same name lies on a disk I didn't look at because it was asleep ({disks}) — have a look there and move it onto the pool.
adv.exclusive_unclear.awake: Perhaps the settings changed after the array started.

adv.exclusive_overflow.title.one: {names} could be exclusive — but for the secondary storage
adv.exclusive_overflow.title.other: {n} shares could be exclusive — but for the secondary storage: {names}

adv.exclusive_overflow.why.one: I couldn't help noticing: this share keeps its data on its pool, and the mover brings back whatever spilled over to the secondary storage. Without a secondary storage it could be an exclusive share — /mnt/user/… a link straight to the pool, past Unraid's FUSE layer, noticeably faster. Worth it only if the pool has room for all of it: without a secondary storage a full pool means a full share. If so: run the mover so everything is on the pool, set «Secondary storage» to «None» in the share's settings, delete what is left of the share on another pool or disk (in brackets; empty folders count too), then stop and start the array. Needs «Permit exclusive shares» (Settings → Global Share Settings).
adv.exclusive_overflow.why.other: I couldn't help noticing: these shares keep their data on their pool, and the mover brings back whatever spilled over to the secondary storage. Without a secondary storage they could be exclusive shares — /mnt/user/… a link straight to the pool, past Unraid's FUSE layer, noticeably faster. Worth it only if the pool has room for all of it: without a secondary storage a full pool means a full share. If so: run the mover so everything is on the pool, set «Secondary storage» to «None» in the share's settings, delete what is left of the share on another pool or disk (in brackets; empty folders count too), then stop and start the array. Needs «Permit exclusive shares» (Settings → Global Share Settings).

adv.compose_build.why.one: Its image is built here from a Dockerfile («build:» in the compose file); no registry has it. Compose Manager's «Update» and «Force Update» pull the images first — that fails here and can leave the containers «Created». Rebuild it instead, in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right): this fetches the newer base image, builds anew and recreates what changed.
adv.compose_build.why.other: Their images are built here from a Dockerfile («build:» in the compose file); no registry has them. Compose Manager's «Update» and «Force Update» pull the images first — that fails here and can leave the containers «Created». Rebuild them instead, in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right): this fetches the newer base image, builds anew and recreates what changed.

adv.cron_dead.title.one: A cron line starts {names} — and that's gone
adv.cron_dead.title.other: Cron lines start {n} programs that are gone: {names}

adv.cron_dead.why: Well, well — leftovers: the plugin ({plugins}) is gone, its line stayed. crond tries every time and fails quietly. Harmless, but untidy — and confusing when you look for what runs when. {how}
adv.cron_dead.own: They are in root's own crontab (crontab -l): the command below removes them in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right) and keeps a copy on the flash first.
adv.cron_dead.system: Lines in /etc/cron.d come from a plugin (Unraid builds its own crontab there from the plugins' .cron files on the flash): reinstall that plugin, or remove it under Plugins.
adv.spindown_default.title: Disks never sleep
adv.spindown_default.why: The default spin down delay is «Never»: every array disk keeps spinning around the clock — power, heat and wear. 30 to 60 minutes is a good start; with pools for appdata and VMs most disks then really rest.
adv.spindown_some.why: Set to «Never» on their own. Fine for a disk that is busy anyway — otherwise it only costs power and wear. Disk settings: click the disk on Main.
adv.old_disks.why: More than about 5 years of running hours. Not a fault — but the time to keep an eye on SMART, have a spare at hand and make sure what's on it is backed up.
adv.parity.title: Last parity check: {when}
adv.parity.why: A regular check (monthly or quarterly) finds bad sectors before a disk fails and you need the parity. Settings → Scheduler → Parity Check, with a time when nobody needs the server.
adv.ups.title: No UPS
adv.ups.why: When the power goes, the server simply stops: open files may break, afterwards Unraid runs a long parity check. A small UPS gives it time to shut down cleanly (Settings → UPS Settings; for a NUT server the NUT plugin).
adv.syslog.title: After a crash the log is gone
adv.syslog.why: Unraid keeps its syslog in RAM — after a crash or a hard reset nobody can read what happened, Ms. Protocolli included. «Mirror syslog to flash» (for a while, it wears the stick) or a syslog server (this one: a share as local syslog folder) keeps it.
adv.security.title: Security is the night watchman's job now
adv.security.why: Shares open to everyone, Telnet, FTP, privileged containers, the CPU's protection — that's his department now, and he notices when something changes, too. Only: he doesn't work here yet. The team lead can hire him. Between us: I would.
